message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can quickly find out your current download/upload speeds yourself. Below are a few methods you can try, depending on what’s available on your machine.

---

## 1. Use a Web‑Based Speed Test (easiest)

1. Open a browser and go to one of the following sites:
   * https://www.speedtest.net/
   * https://fast.com/ (Netflix’s simple test)
   * https://www.fastestinternet.com/
2. Click the “Go” or “Start” button.  
   The page will download a small file from a nearby server and report:
   * **Download speed** (Mbps)
   * **Upload speed** (Mbps)
   * **Ping / latency** (ms)

These sites are reliable and give you a quick snapshot of your current bandwidth.

---

## 2. Run a Speed Test from the Command Line

If you prefer a terminal or want to automate the test, you can use **speedtest‑cli** (Python‑based) or the official Speedtest CLI from Ookla.

### 2.1. Using `speedtest-cli` (Python)

1. **Install it** (if you have Python and pip):

   ```bash
   pip install speedtest-cli
   ```

2. **Run it**:

   ```bash
   speedtest-cli --simple
   ```

   Output will look like:

   ```
   Host: isp.example.com
   Ping: 12.34 ms
   Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
   Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
   ```

### 2.2. Using Ookla’s Official CLI

1. **Download** the binary for Windows from https://www.speedtest.net/apps/cli
2. **Run** it from PowerShell or CMD:

   ```powershell
   .\speedtest.exe
   ```

   or

   ```cmd
   speedtest.exe
   ```

   It will automatically pick the nearest server and display the results.

---

## 3. Quick PowerShell One‑Liner (If you have `Invoke-WebRequest`)

If you don’t want to install anything, you can use PowerShell to download a file from a known server and calculate the speed manually:

```powershell
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$start = Get-Date
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin"
$end = Get-Date
$bytes = (Get-Item "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin").Length
$seconds = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes / 1MB) / $seconds
Write-Host "Download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbit/s"
Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin"
```

> **Note:** This method only measures download speed. Upload speed would require a different approach (e.g., uploading a file to a server you control).

---

## 4. Check Network Adapter Statistics (Windows)

If you just want to see the *current* link speed (e.g., 100 Mbps vs. 1 Gbps), you can inspect the adapter:

```powershell
Get-NetAdapter | Format-Table Name, Status, LinkSpeed
```

This tells you the negotiated link speed, not the actual throughput.

---

## 5. Automate with a Batch Script (Optional)

If you want a quick batch file that runs the official Speedtest CLI and logs the result:

```batch
@echo off
set LOG=%USERPROFILE%\speedtest_%date:~-4%%date:~4,2%%date:~7,2%.txt
speedtest.exe --format=json > "%LOG%"
echo Results saved to %LOG%
pause
```

Place this next to `speedtest.exe` and double‑click to run.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | Best For | How to Run |
|--------|----------|------------|
| Browser (speedtest.net, fast.com) | One‑time, quick | Open site, click “Go” |
| `speedtest-cli` (Python) | Terminal, scripting | `pip install speedtest-cli` → `speedtest-cli --simple` |
| Ookla CLI (official) | Accurate, cross‑platform | Download → `speedtest.exe` |
| PowerShell one‑liner | No install, quick download test | Paste script into PowerShell |
| `Get-NetAdapter` | Link speed only | `Get-NetAdapter | Format-Table Name, Status, LinkSpeed` |

Pick the one that fits your workflow. If you run into any issues (e.g., “command not found”), let me know and I can help troubleshoot!
